encounters.cc: Increased urinary frequency, urgency, and burning sensation during urination

lines: Increased urinary frequency, urgency, and burning sensation during urination
She presents to the clinic complaining of a 6-month history of increased urinary frequency, urgency, and a burning sensation during urination.
She also reports experiencing recurrent urinary tract infections and mild urinary incontinence that has worsened over the past few months.
She has tried over-the-counter cranberry supplements and increased water intake with no improvement in symptoms.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 52, no hormone replacement therapy)
- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)
Her past medical history is significant for hypertension, which is well-controlled with hydrochlorothiazide.
She underwent menopause at the age of 52 and has not used hormone replacement therapy.
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Retired administrative assistant.
On physical examination, the external genitalia appear atrophic with pale, thin vulvar skin.
Vaginal mucosa is dry and lacks rugae.
There is no vaginal discharge or bleeding, and bimanual examination is unremarkable.
Urinalysis shows no evidence of infection.

encounters.cc: 6-month history of sudden, overwhelming urges to urinate resulting in occasional incontinence

lines: 6-month history of sudden, overwhelming urges to urinate resulting in occasional incontinence
The patient presents to Urology for further evaluation of urinary symptoms previously assessed in Internal Medicine three months prior.
She reports that these symptoms are affecting her quality of life, as she is now hesitant to leave her house for extended periods.
She has tried to manage her symptoms by reducing her caffeine intake and scheduling regular bathroom breaks every 2 hours, but she has not noticed any improvement.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 52, no hormone replacement therapy)
- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)
Her past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus, well-controlled on metformin, and hypertension, managed with lisinopril.
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Retired administrative assistant.
On physical examination, her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no palpable masses.
A pelvic examination reveals no prolapse or noticeable abnormalities.
Urinalysis is negative for infection, glucose, or protein.
Post-void residual volume is within normal limits.

encounters.cc: Discomfort in mouth with difficulty eating and occasional speech interference

lines: Discomfort in mouth with difficulty eating and occasional speech interference

The patient presents for ENT evaluation of oral discomfort that has been progressively worsening over the past year, continuing longitudinal care for diabetes and hypertension following recent urology and internal medicine encounters.
She reports difficulty with eating and occasional speech interference.
She mentions that she has been considering getting dentures due to recent tooth loss but is concerned about the fit because of this oral mass.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 52, no hormone replacement therapy)
- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)
She has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, which are well-controlled.
She takes metformin and lisinopril, respectively.
She is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol.
On examination, you note a hard, midline mass on the roof of her mouth, which is non-tender to palpation.
The mass does not blanch with pressure and the overlying mucosa is intact without ulceration.
The rest of the oral cavity examination is unremarkable.

encounters.cc: Ongoing issues with urine leakage gradually worsened over the past eight months

lines: Ongoing issues with urine leakage gradually worsened over the past eight months
The patient is a 58-year-old postmenopausal female who returns to the urology clinic for further evaluation of progressive urinary urgency and involuntary leakage.

Following her initial presentation to Internal Medicine in January 2020 and subsequent assessment in this department in April 2020 for similar symptoms, she now reports worsening over the intervening eight months.

She reports that the episodes typically begin with a sudden, intense sensation of needing to urinate, which she describes as coming "out of nowhere." Often, she is unable to make it to the bathroom in time, resulting in involuntary leakage of moderate amounts of urine.
These events have become increasingly disruptive, occurring several times during the day and occasionally at night.
She has tried to cut back on fluids, but the urgency remains unchanged.
She does not experience leakage when sneezing, laughing, or exercising, and she denies any sensation of incomplete bladder emptying or dribbling after voiding.
There is no associated dysuria, hematuria, or pelvic discomfort.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 52, no hormone replacement therapy)
- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)
Her medical history includes mild hypertension. She is postmenopausal.
She has never undergone pelvic surgery.
She takes she takes a low-dose thiazide diuretic.
She lives independently and remains active in her community, although she has started to avoid outings due to fear of accidents.
Pelvic examination shows normal tissue tone and no pelvic organ prolapse.
Urinalysis is negative for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, blood, or glucose.
Patient presents with persistent cough during urologic care.
She reports that the cough is nonproductive and is not associated with dyspnea, wheezing, or chest pain.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 52, no hormone replacement therapy)
- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)
She has a past medical history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Her medications include lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin.
On physical examination, her blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats per minute, and respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute.
Lung auscultation reveals no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
The rest of the examination is unremarkable.

encounters.cc: 3-day history of fever, shortness of breath, and dry cough

lines: 3-day history of fever, shortness of breath, and dry cough
Patient with incontinence and prior pulmonary evaluation returning with acute symptoms.
She reports that her symptoms began a week after she started taking a new medication for a urinary tract infection.
She denies any recent travel or sick contacts.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 52, no hormone replacement therapy)
- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)
Her past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension.
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Retired administrative assistant.
On examination, she is febrile with a temperature of 38.5°C (101.3°F), her heart rate is 102 beats per minute, and her respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute.
Oxygen saturation is 92% on room air.
Lung auscultation reveals bilateral basilar crackles.
A diffuse erythematous rash is noted on her trunk and upper extremities.
- White blood cell count: 12,000/mm³ with a normal differential
Chest X-ray shows bilateral basilar opacities and small pleural effusions.

lines: Painful rash on left flank present for three days

- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)

encounters.cc: Severe burning pain on the left side of her chest for three days

lines: Severe burning pain on the left side of her chest for three days
The patient returns six months after her prior zoster episode with a history of varicella zoster virus infection.
She describes the pain as a constant, burning sensation that has been present for the past three days.
She denies any recent trauma or injury to the area.
- Postmenopausal status (menopause at age 52, no hormone replacement therapy)
- History of varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox)
Her medical history is significant for hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
She had chickenpox as a child.
She takes for which she takes hydrochlorothiazide, and type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with metformin.
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Retired administrative assistant.
Her vital signs are within normal limits.
On physical examination, you note hyperesthesia over the affected area but no rash is evident.
